The Descent Protocol

# The Descent Protocol

## Discovered work is governed work, and it goes one level deep

*Deployed as `docs/governance/protocols/descent.md`. Depends on `docs/governance/protocols/root-cause.md` and `docs/governance/protocols/correction-loop.md`.*

## Purpose

An agent working a task discovers a defect nobody raised. Fixing it
is often the right call — the cause is fresh, the context is loaded, and
deferring it means someone rebuilds that understanding later.
**This protocol does not exist to stop discovered work.**

It exists because discovered work fails in two specific ways, and
both are invisible while they are happening.

**Recursion.** The discovered defect leads to another,
which leads to another. Every descent is individually justified — each
one genuinely blocks the level above, each one is genuinely real. Three
levels down, nobody can state the original task, every level is
half-finished, and the return path exists only in one agent's context
window. Chasing white rabbits is not a failure of judgment at any single
step; it is the absence of a limit.

**Exemption.** Discovered work arrives ungoverned. The
same agent that would produce a diagnosis artifact for an assigned
defect fixes a discovered one with no artifact, no spec, no caller. Not
from dishonesty — the protocols read as governing *tasks*, and
this was not a task, it was something noticed. The category feels
different, so the rules feel inapplicable.

The two failures are independent and both must be closed. Unlimited
depth with perfect compliance is still a rabbit hole where everything is
beautifully specified and the original work is abandoned. Depth 1 with
an exemption is one unspecified fix landing inside someone else's diff,
every time.

### The three controls

| | Answers | Mechanism |

| Depth | How far may this go? | A hard limit of 1, counted per chain, reset only on verified return |

| Non-exemption | What governs it once it does? | Nothing distinguishes discovered work from assigned work except an integer |

| Separation | Where does it land? | Its own scope declaration, its own commit — never merged into the parent's diff |

Separation is what makes the other two enforceable. A depth-1 fix
hidden inside a depth-0 diff is invisible to every existing gate no
matter how well it complies.

### The rule, in one line

**Discovery confers no authority.** Work an agent found
is governed identically to work it was given — same spec, same
acceptance criteria, same root cause requirement for defects, same
caller requirement, same scope declaration, same commit separation.
There is no lighter path for something you noticed yourself, and there
is no third level.

### Scope and dependencies

Every task, in any application, attended or unattended, by any
author. This protocol adds no new governance of its own: it depends on
the **Root Cause Protocol** for defect-class work and the
**Correction Loop** for everything else, and its entire job
is to ensure both apply at depth 1 exactly as they do at depth 0.

**What it guarantees.** That a chain of discovered work
terminates, that the return to the original task is verified rather than
assumed, and that no unit of work is governed differently because of who
raised it.

**What it does not guarantee.** That the discovered
defect was worth fixing, or that the judgment to descend was right. It
bounds the cost of being wrong rather than preventing it.

## Depth

Every unit of work carries a depth. It is one integer on the work
record and it is the only thing distinguishing discovered work from
assigned work.

| Depth | What it is | May proceed? |

| 0 | Assigned work — a task from the backlog, a finding from intake | Yes, under the usual protocols |

| 1 | Something discovered while working depth 0 | Yes, if it satisfies every requirement depth 0 does |

| 2+ | Something discovered while working depth 1 | Never. Captured, not worked |

### The limit is 1, and it is a hard stop

Not a guideline, not a default, not something an agent weighs against
the value of what it found. This is the one control in the whole design
that cannot be a judgment call, because **at every level the argument to continue is sound.** That is the nature of the
failure: each descent is justified on its own terms, which is why
judgment never stops it.

Depth 2 sounds like a reasonable compromise and is where the rabbit
hole actually begins — at depth 2 the return path to depth 0 is already
something nobody is tracking. Start at 1. Raise it only if the capture
rate shows it is demonstrably too tight, and treat that as a measured
decision rather than a concession made in the moment.

### Depth is per chain, not per session

A chain is a descent and its return. It opens when an agent leaves
depth 0 for discovered work and closes when it returns to depth 0 with
the discovered work either completed or abandoned.

An agent that finishes its depth-1 fix, returns to depth 0, and later
discovers something else opens a **fresh chain at depth 1**. That is not recursion — that is a productive day, and the
protocol should not punish it. The counter resets on verified return,
never on elapsed time, and never because the agent believes it has moved
on.

```
flowchart LR
A["Depth 0<br/>assigned task"] --> B{"Discovery"}
B -->|"specifiable"| C["Depth 1<br/>full protocols apply"]
B -->|"not specifiable"| X["Capture"]
C --> D{"Discovery at depth 1"}
D --> X
C --> E["Return to depth 0<br/>verified"]
E --> A
```

The diagram has no path from depth 1 to depth 2. That absence is the
protocol.

### Depth 1 is permission to work, not permission to skip

Saying discovered work *may* proceed is not the interesting
half. What makes depth 1 legitimate is that it carries every obligation
depth 0 carries — spec, acceptance criteria, root cause for defects,
caller for capabilities, scope declaration, separate commit. Section 4
states this in full, because it is the half that gets lost.

A discovered defect that cannot meet those obligations is not blocked
by this protocol. It is blocked by the protocols that already exist, and
the correct outcome is capture.

## Return

A depth limit without a verified return is half a control. An agent
that descends once, completes the depth-1 work perfectly, and never
resumes the original task has not recursed — it has abandoned, and the
outcome is the same: the assigned work did not ship.

**The chain is the unit, and it closes on return.**
Opening a chain is a recorded event naming what is being left; closing
it is a recorded event showing the return happened. Both are cheap and
both are machine-checkable.

### The stack must be explicit

Before descending, the agent states what it is returning to — the
depth-0 item id, and the state it is in. Holding that only in context is
the failure: context is exactly what a long descent degrades, and an
agent three hours into a discovered defect has no reliable memory of
what it interrupted.

This is one line on the chain record. It exists so the return can be
verified by something other than the agent's recollection.

### Blocked at depth 1 means stop, not descend

The hardest rule in the protocol, and the one that carries the most
weight.

If the depth-1 fix genuinely cannot complete without a depth-2 fix,
do not descend. **Abandon depth 1, capture both, return to depth 0.**

The reasoning is not stubbornness. Being blocked at depth 1 is
evidence that the depth-1 diagnosis was wrong — the cause sits further
up than the agent thought, and the depth-2 item is probably the real
one. Descending compounds a diagnostic error rather than resolving it,
and it does so at the moment the agent is least able to notice, because
the blocking relationship feels like proof that the analysis was
right.

This will feel wrong in the moment, every time. That is expected and
it is not a reason to relax it. "I cannot finish this without that" is
the sentence that produces every three-level chain, and it is true every
time it is said.

### What return requires

| Condition | Return is |

| Depth-1 work completed, its commit landed under its own scope | Clean — close the chain, resume depth 0 |

| Depth-1 work abandoned, findings captured | Clean — close the chain, resume depth 0 |

| Depth-1 work incomplete and still open | Not a return. The chain stays open and counts against the metric |

| Agent moves to unrelated depth-0 work without closing | Abandonment. Recorded as such |

The distinction in the last two rows is the one worth instrumenting.
An agent that drifts from depth 1 into something else entirely is the
failure this protocol targets, and without a chain record it looks
identical to finishing.

### The measurement

**Chains opened versus chains returned to origin.** This
is the single number that says whether the protocol works, and it is
more informative than the depth limit itself — a fleet that never
exceeds depth 1 but returns on half its chains is losing assigned work
at scale.

Report open chain age too. A chain open for a long time is a descent
that became the task, which is the failure mode arriving by a slower
route.

## No exemptions at any depth

Depth 1 work is subject to every requirement depth 0 work is subject
to. This is not a reminder that the rules still apply — it is a
statement that **there are no two kinds of work.** There is
work, and it carries a depth field, and nothing else in the record
distinguishes discovered from assigned.

That construction is deliberate. If discovered work produced a
different *kind* of record, an exemption could attach to the
kind, and an agent could reason its way into one honestly. Same record,
one extra integer: there is nothing for an exemption to attach to.

### The obligations, in full

| Requirement | Depth 0 | Depth 1 |

| Spec stating behaviour under constraints | Required | Required |

| Executable acceptance criterion, recorded failing first | Required | Required |

| Root cause artifact, if defect-class | Required | Required |

| A caller inside the system, if capability-class | Required | Required |

| Declared file scope | Required | Required |

| Its own commit | Required | Required |

| Watching window before closure | Required | Required |

No row differs. That is the section.

### The exemption routes, named and shut

Each of these is a real argument that an agent will construct in good
faith. Naming them is what stops them being invented fresh each
time.

**"It's the same file — it's practically in scope."**
Proximity is not scope. The declared file set was written against a
specification; a second change to the same file serves a different one.
Scope is defined by intent, not by path adjacency.

**"It's two lines, a spec would be absurd."** If it is
genuinely two lines, the spec is one sentence and the acceptance
criterion is one test — which is cheap, not absurd. If neither can be
written that briefly, the change was not as small as it looked. The size
of the diff is not evidence about the size of the claim.

**"I couldn't proceed without it."** Then it is either
in scope for the current task, in which case amend the scope declaration
on the record and continue at the same depth, or it is a separate item,
in which case it is depth 1 with full obligations. Blocking never
creates an exemption; it only decides which of those two is true. At
depth 1 this argument means abandon and return — see section 3.

**"It's obviously right, no spec needed."** Obviousness
is the reported experience of an agent that has not yet been
contradicted. It is also present in exactly the same strength on the
changes that turn out wrong. If it is obvious, writing it down costs
seconds.

**"While I was in here anyway."** The efficiency is real
and the cost lands on the reviewer, who now reads a diff containing two
unrelated intentions and reviews neither properly. The saving is the
agent's; the expense is someone else's.

**"Nobody raised it, so it isn't governed."** This is
the root of all the others. Governance attaches to the work, not to who
noticed it.

### Where enforcement comes from

Nothing new. The Root Cause Protocol and the Correction Loop gate at
the commit boundary and neither asks who raised the item — a commit is
refused for a missing diagnosis artifact or an uncalled capability
regardless of depth. **The gates already cannot be exempted; they simply have to be reached**, which is what section 5 is for.

The one thing this section adds is the depth field on the work
record, so that compliance can be measured separately at depth 0 and
depth 1. Expect them to differ at first — and that gap, rather than any
single violation, is the measurement that says whether the exemption
instinct is real in your fleet.

## Separation

The third control, and the one that makes the first two enforceable.
A depth-1 fix merged into the depth-0 diff is invisible to every gate in
the system no matter how well it complies, because the gates read the
commit and the commit says it is the parent task.

**Depth-1 work lands as its own commit, against its own declared scope, referencing its parent by id.** Never inside the
parent's diff.

### Why this is the load-bearing piece

The Correction Loop already declares a file scope per item and
already flags a diff touching paths outside it. That check is the entire
detection mechanism for drift — and it fails silently if two items share
one commit, because the union of two scopes covers everything either one
touches.

So separation is not hygiene. It is the precondition for the existing
control to work at all.

### The commit record

A depth-1 commit carries two extra trailers alongside the ones the
other protocols require:

```
Depth: 1
Parent: QOS-1234
Scope: scripts/fleet/test-gate.mjs
Caller: scheduler:hourly("settlement-expiry")
```

`Parent` is what lets the chain be reconstructed from git
alone, without the work tracker. `Depth` is what lets
compliance be measured separately at each level, per section 4.

### What the gate refuses

| Condition | Outcome |

| Diff touches paths outside the declared scope, single item | Refused. Either drift, or undeclared discovered work |

| Commit carries `Depth: 1` with no `Parent` | Refused. An orphan chain cannot be returned from |

| Commit carries `Depth: 2` or higher | Refused. No such work is permitted |

| `Parent` names an item that is not open | Refused. Descending from finished work is not a chain |

| Two item ids referenced in one commit | Refused. Split it |

All of these are mechanical and all of them run in CI, where they
bind regardless of which CLI, model or orchestrator produced the
work.

### The split path

Refusal has to leave a cheap route forward or it becomes something
people work around. When a diff breaks scope, the agent's options
are:

- Amend the scope declaration , if the extra paths genuinely serve the current specification. Recorded, reviewable, and the right answer more often than people expect — an incomplete initial scope is common and is not drift.

- Split the commit , if the extra paths serve a different intention. The second commit opens depth 1 and takes the full obligations.

- Revert the extra paths and capture , if the second intention cannot be specified.

Option 1 is the one worth watching. It is correct and it is also the
obvious bypass — an agent that amends scope after every discovery has
converted a hard control into a formality. Count amendments per item; a
rising rate is the signal, not any single one.

## Capture

Capture is the exit for everything the limit excludes: discoveries
made at depth 1, and discoveries at depth 0 that cannot be specified. It
is the cheap path, and it has to genuinely be cheap or the controls
above become unsurvivable.

**The ratio that decides everything: capturing must cost less than fixing.** Every failure of this protocol is that ratio
inverting. If filing takes longer than a two-line edit, the edit
happens. If captured items visibly go nowhere, capture stops feeling
real and the edit happens. Sections 2 to 5 are only as strong as this is
easy.

### One action

```
qos capture --locus scripts/fleet/test-gate.mjs --severity high
"test-gate returns skip when node_modules is absent"
```

Everything else is derived: the parent item, the depth it was found
at, the chain, the agent, the commit in progress, the timestamp. The
agent supplies a sentence, a path, and a severity. If capture ever needs
more than that, it is too expensive and will be skipped.

Capture never blocks. It does not open a dialog, wait for triage, or
require the current work to pause. The agent captures and continues
inside the same action.

### The record

| Field | From |

| Statement | Agent, one sentence |

| Locus | Agent, a path or symbol |

| Severity | Agent, rated against the rubric in section 7 |

| Depth found at, parent item, chain id | Derived |

| Observing agent, mode, timestamp | Derived |

| Signature | Derived, so intake can dedupe it |

The derived signature matters: a capture matching an existing open
finding increments that finding's recurrence counter rather than
creating a duplicate, exactly as the Correction Loop's intake does for
detector-raised issues.

### Capture is not a promise

A captured observation enters triage. It is not a commitment to fix,
and the protocol should not imply otherwise — a capture store that
pretends everything in it will be worked becomes a graveyard, and a
visible graveyard is what teaches agents that capture is theatre.

What capture guarantees is that the observation is counted, deduped,
and ordered against everything else. Section 7 covers the ordering;
section 8 covers what happens to the things that lose.

### The capture rate is a diagnostic

Watch it in both directions.

**Near zero** means agents are not capturing — either
nothing is being discovered, which is implausible in any real codebase,
or discoveries are being fixed inline and the separation gate is not
catching them. Check the scope-amendment rate before believing the first
reading.

**Very high with a flat triage rate** means capture has
become a way to discharge responsibility. Everything gets filed, nothing
gets worked, and the store grows until nobody reads it.

The healthy signal is a steady capture rate with a proportionate flow
out of triage — which is a property of section 8 rather than of capture
itself.

## Severity and triage

Captured observations are ordered the way reported defects are
ordered anywhere else: by severity, against product work rather than in
a queue of their own.

| Severity | Definition | Priority |

| S1 | Data loss, security exposure, or a control that silently permits what it exists to refuse | Preempts product work |

| S2 | A capability is wrong or absent in production and no mechanism will notice | Preempts product work |

| S3 | Defect with a workaround, or a mechanism that works but reports nothing | Below product work |

| S4 | Correctness-neutral: clarity, consistency, tidying | Below S3; expires if not pulled |

The definitions are tied to impact rather than effort, deliberately.
How long something takes to fix is an argument for scheduling it, never
for its severity, and conflating the two is how a two-line change
acquires urgency it has not earned.

### The observer's rating is suspect

An agent that wanted to fix something and was refused has an obvious
interest in rating it S1, because S1 is the route back to working on it
now. Left unchecked, the preemption path becomes the drift path and the
depth limit is bypassed by inflation rather than by argument.

Three guards:

**Evidence, not adjectives.** A rating names what it
rests on — the control that permits the wrong thing, the production
behaviour that is wrong, the workaround that exists. "This looks
serious" is not a rating. An S1 with no evidence field is downgraded
automatically rather than rejected, because rejection just teaches
agents to write the evidence field carelessly.

**Re-rated at intake by something that did not observe it.** In attended mode, the person. In unattended mode, the
orchestrator — never the observing agent, and never the agent that goes
on to work the item. Both ratings are kept: the observer's and the
triage rating, separately.

**Self-assigned-high rate, per agent.** The gap between
an agent's own S1/S2 rate and the rate that survives re-rating is the
measurement. One inflated rating is noise; a consistent gap is an agent
that has learned the route, and it is visible in a way no single
decision is.

### Preemption is bounded

S1 and S2 displacing product work is correct and is itself an
interruption mechanism — the same shape as the task-level drift this
protocol prevents, one layer up. A burst of high-rated captures can
stall delivery entirely while every individual preemption looks
justified.

So cap it: a limit on how much in-flight product work may be
displaced at once, set per application. When the cap is reached, further
S1 and S2 items queue behind the ones already preempting rather than
adding to them. The cap being hit is itself a finding — either something
is badly wrong, or ratings are inflating.

### What triage produces

A captured observation leaves triage in one of three states:

| Outcome | Meaning |

| Promoted | Enters the Correction Loop at step 1 as a finding, with its severity setting its position |

| Merged | Matched an existing finding; the counter incremented and the capture closed |

| Parked | Recorded, deduped, counted, not scheduled. Subject to section 8 |

Parked is the honest outcome for most S4s and many S3s, and it has to
be visibly normal. A triage process where everything is promoted is one
that has stopped discriminating, and the queue it feeds will be ignored
within a month.

## Expiry

The capture store's failure mode is not overflow. It is becoming a
place where observations go to be forgotten while everyone still calls
it a backlog — and once agents can see that, capture stops being a real
alternative to fixing inline, which collapses the whole protocol back to
where it started.

The fix is to make expiry explicit rather than letting it happen
silently.

### Parked items expire

| Severity | Horizon | On expiry |

| S1, S2 | Never park — promoted at triage | — |

| S3 | 90 days parked | Expires; counted |

| S4 | 30 days parked | Expires; counted |

Expiry is deletion with a tally, not archival. An archive is a
graveyard with better branding: it has the same effect on behaviour,
because what agents respond to is whether parked items are ever worked,
not whether their text still exists somewhere.

**The recurrence counter overrides the horizon.** An
expired signature that is captured again does not start over — it
returns with its accumulated count, and a count that keeps climbing is
the evidence that the horizon was wrong for that item. This is what
stops expiry discarding something real: the codebase keeps re-raising
it, and the counter makes that visible.

### Expiry is reported, not silent

A periodic report names what expired, at what severity, and with what
recurrence count. Two readings matter:

- Expiring at S3 with a rising recurrence count — the horizon is too short, or the rating was too low. This is the case where a real problem is being discarded repeatedly.

- Expiring at S4 with a count of one — the system is working exactly as intended. Most tidying observations are correct, unimportant, and should go.

### What this buys

The store stays small enough that a person can read it, which is the
only condition under which triage decisions stay honest. A parked list
of forty items gets reviewed; a parked list of four hundred gets a
filter, and then gets ignored.

It also makes parking a defensible answer rather than a euphemism. An
agent told its observation was parked knows the item is counted, will be
re-raised by recurrence if it matters, and will otherwise disappear —
which is a truthful description of what happens to most small
observations in any engineering organisation, and is more trustworthy
than a promise nobody intends to keep.

## Attended and unattended

Mode is declared, never inferred, exactly as in the Correction Loop.
Fleet and orchestrator runs are always unattended. A run with no
declared mode refuses to start; if a fallback is unavoidable it falls
back to unattended.

**The depth limit does not vary by mode.** This is worth
stating because the temptation runs the other way — a person is present,
they can judge whether the third level is warranted, so why not let
them. Because the recursion failure is not caused by absent judgment.
Every level of every rabbit hole was entered by someone exercising
judgment, and an attended agent asking permission to descend will get
it, because the argument is always good. The limit protects attended
sessions from the same failure and it holds identically.

What mode changes is who decides the things that are genuinely
decisions.

| Decision point | Attended | Unattended default |

| Is this specifiable enough to work at depth 1? | Agent proposes; person decides | Can the agent write a spec and an executable acceptance criterion? If not, capture |

| Defect or capability | Person decides | Prior art: ever worked → defect; no caller ever existed → capability |

| Severity at capture | Agent rates; person re-rates | Agent rates against the rubric; orchestrator re-rates |

| Scope amendment vs split | Person decides | Do the extra paths serve the current specification? If not, split |

| Blocked at depth 1 | Abandon and return. Not the person's call | Abandon and return |

| Triage outcome | Person | Orchestrator, by severity and the preemption cap |

| Depth limit exceeded | Refused | Refused |

Two rows are the same in both columns on purpose. Abandoning at depth
1 and the depth limit itself are not decisions — they are the protocol,
and exposing them to judgment in attended mode would remove the only
control that is not an argument.

### Recording

Every defaulted decision carries the decision point, the branch
taken, the evidence that selected it, and the mode — recorded the same
way a person's decision is, and distinguishable from one. Reviewing six
weeks later why an item was worked at depth 1 rather than captured,
*a default fired on specifiability* and *someone decided*
are different facts with different reliability.

### The escape

There is no new escape hatch here. An unattended agent never blocks
waiting for a person: it captures, returns, and continues. The only
route to a person is the Correction Loop's existing floor — five
attempts on a class routes the finding to the Needs You queue — and the
descent protocol does not add to it.

A chain that cannot be closed is the one case worth flagging
separately: if an agent cannot return to depth 0 because the depth-0
item no longer exists or its branch is gone, the chain closes as
`orphaned` and is counted. It does not wake anyone.

## Enforcement, measurement, open decisions

### What binds where

| Control | Enforced by | Strength |

| Depth limit | `Depth:` trailer; commit refused above 1 | Mechanical |

| Parent linkage | `Parent:` trailer must name an open item | Mechanical |

| Separation | One item id per commit; scope check | Mechanical |

| No exemptions | Existing Root Cause and Correction Loop gates | Mechanical |

| Chain return | Chain record; open-chain report | Mechanical, after the fact |

| Capture instead of descend | Nothing refuses a decision not to capture | Behavioural |

The last row is the honest limit. An agent that discovers something
at depth 1 and simply says nothing leaves no trace — there is no
artifact whose absence can be detected, because the absence is of an
observation. The lever is that capture is cheap and that the alternative
(a scope-breaking commit) is refused, not that silence is caught.

Uniform exit codes: `0` passed, `1` refused
with the offending trailer or path named, `2` the check could
not run. **Exit 2 blocks**, as everywhere else.

### The numbers

| Metric | Reading |

| Chains returned to origin / chains opened | The headline. Below 1 means assigned work is being abandoned |

| Open chain age | A chain open a long time is a descent that became the task |

| Depth-1 compliance vs depth-0 compliance | The gap is the exemption instinct, measured |

| Self-assigned-high rate per agent | Observer ratings that do not survive re-rating |

| Scope amendments per item | Rising means the split rule has become a formality |

| Capture rate | Near zero means inline fixing; very high with flat triage means discharge |

| Parked expiring with rising recurrence | The horizon or the rating was wrong |

| Preemption cap hits | Either something is badly wrong or ratings are inflating |

**Two suspicious zeros.** No captures at all, and no
depth-1 work at all. The first means discoveries are being fixed inline;
the second means they are being suppressed, and an agent that never
descends is not more disciplined, it is one that has stopped
reporting.

### Build order

| | Work | Note |

| 1 | `Depth` and `Parent` trailers; commit gate refusing depth ≥ 2 and orphan chains | The hard stop, and it is cheap |

| 2 | One-item-per-commit check | Makes the existing scope check work |

| 3 | `qos capture`, one command, deriving everything it can | Must land before 1 is enforced, or there is no exit |

| 4 | Chain record: open, close, orphan; open-chain report | Return becomes measurable |

| 5 | Severity rubric and re-rating at intake | |

| 6 | Triage into the Correction Loop, preemption cap | |

| 7 | Parked expiry and the expiry report | |

| 8 | Depth-split compliance metrics | Tells you whether the exemption instinct is real here |

**Step 3 before step 1.** Enforcing the limit without a
working capture path leaves agents with no legitimate move, and what
they will do instead is fix inline and hope the scope check misses
it.

### Open decisions

**A — Is the limit 1 everywhere, or per application?**
Argued as 1 throughout. A case exists for 2 in exploratory or greenfield
work where the dependency structure is genuinely unknown. I would not
open that door initially: per-application depth limits will be set to 2
by whoever is most frustrated, and the frustration is the symptom the
limit exists to produce.

**B — Does a human-raised discovery at depth 0 count as depth 1?** If you notice something mid-session and ask the agent to fix
it, is that assigned work or discovered work? I would call it depth 0 —
a new assigned item — because you raised it, and the chain concept does
not apply. But it means a person can generate unbounded depth by asking
repeatedly, and whether that matters is yours to decide.

**C — Preemption cap value.** Named as necessary, not
set. Needs a number per application.

**D — Does the protocol apply to non-code work?** A
spec, a runbook, a config change. The trailers work; the root-cause
requirement is awkward. Probably yes with the defect-class rules
relaxed, but it has not been thought through here.

### The honest limit

This protocol does not make discovered work good. It bounds how far a
wrong judgment propagates and ensures the work is governed the same way
regardless of who raised it. The judgment about whether to descend at
all stays with the agent, and it will sometimes be wrong — which is
acceptable, because one level of wrong is recoverable and three is
not.

If after two cycles the chain-return rate is at or near 1 and depth-1
compliance matches depth-0, the protocol has done its job and the
remaining machinery is worth trimming rather than extending.

> as one thing.
The depth limit, parent linkage, separation and the return half are all built. Severity, triage and expiry are not.

| Control | State | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Depth limit, refused above 1 | ENFORCED | B-11226 |
| Parent must name an open item | ENFORCED | B-11226 |
| One item id per commit | ENFORCED | B-11226 |
| Scope trailer | ENFORCED | B-11226; a diff outside the declared scope is refused, and an unreadable diff refuses rather than passes |
| Chain record: open, close, orphan | BUILT | B-11226; opened by the descent gate on a passing depth-1 commit |
| Open-chain report | BUILT | Invoked at session close. Reports and does not block by design: a chain open at close is often legitimate, and refusing the close would make every multi-session descent unclosable. |
| capture, one command | BUILT | B-11232; scripts/backlog/capture.mjs |
| Severity rubric and re-rating at intake | BUILT | B-11276. S1-S4 plus all three guards. Capture takes --severity and --evidence, defaulting to S4; an S1 with no evidence is downgraded, not rejected; both ratings are kept |
| Triage: promoted, merged, parked | BUILT | B-11276. MERGED reuses the Correction Loop's step-1 matcher rather than a second notion of sameness. S1 and S2 never park |
| Parked expiry and the expiry report | BUILT | B-11276. S3 90 days, S4 30. Reports rather than deletes: deletion is destructive and the operator's to run |

## Complying with this protocol, before you write

> Run `node scripts/governance/obligations.mjs --files <what you are about to touch>` first. It returns
> what binds this change, deterministically and at no model cost, instead of asking you to carry the
> document. Being refused later is not compliance.

- An item id minted during this session is discovered work: declare `Depth: 1` and `Parent: <open item>`, or `Assigned: <who handed it to you>`.
- The limit is one level. A second descent from discovered work is the chain the limit exists to stop.
- Before rewriting anything a vanished worktree held, run `node scripts/fleet/salvage-reclaim.mjs --item <ID>`. Four reapers capture into stashes and nothing read them back until 2026-09-25; retyping work a capture already holds is churn that looks like progress.

### Deviations, with reasons

**Capture takes two inputs, not three.** The document's form is `--locus`, a statement and `--severity`, and it derives a signature so intake can dedupe the capture against existing findings. The implementation takes locus and statement, derives no signature, and therefore cannot increment an existing finding's recurrence counter.

**Measured cost: about 5.7 seconds per capture** on this repository, nearly all of it git reads against a 33 GB object store. The first implementation took 27.9 seconds because it waited on an allocator that needs 55 seconds here and validated its input afterwards. That number is the protocol: if it climbs, the ratio the document calls decisive inverts and the limit stops being followed.

**The chain closes manually.** Opening is automatic, at the only moment the information exists. Detecting a RETURN automatically - an agent resuming its depth-0 item - is not built, so a chain stays open until something closes it explicitly. The report therefore over-counts open chains rather than under-counting them, which is the safe direction for a measure of abandonment but is not the same as measuring it.

### Not built

The chain record is the half that measures whether the agent came back. Without it, an agent that descends once and never returns is indistinguishable from one that finished, which the document names as the failure the protocol targets.
